I played 4 episodes so far and I have to say this...This game won't get any worse

First of all, the gameplay is simple, yet it makes you feel important because you choose how the characters are seen by ORWELL. Speaking of the characters: They are so good, despite only seeing text, they really do grow on you and each feels different. For example I like who I never thought I'd like and I hate some characters with passion, which is telling about the game's writing because again it's mainly text based. I also like the "conspiracy" web you create, seeing all the relationships making you feel like everything is connected.

After episode 3 everything hit the fan and it's really interesting that you actually start feeling like you're doing the right thing despite the fact you are spying on people, Which is really interesting because most games about government spying makes you feel bad or being on the opposite side.

I can only recommend this game, it was worth to buy the deluxe edition for the soundtrack and I hope there will be a season 2. If you like heavy stories that make you think, buy this game.

I'll keep it short and sweet.  This is a compelling and interesting game.  If you like games like the Stanley Parable, Her Story, Gone Home, etc, then this is for you.  You have more influence in Orwell than you do in the games I have previously mentioned.  It is also the game for our times.  It explores the use, abuse and misuse of the data found online, and how this can influence the lives of the everyday person.  

Well worth playing.

[b] Orwell [/b]

First of, the game "Orwell" is based on the worldwidly popular novel "1984" by George Orwell, whose surname was picked as the game title and which is set in a totalitarian surveillance state. The game is one of the few games that are being released these days that feature unique gameplay and new ideas, although it's not as popular as it would deserve to be. I, however, bought this game during a recent Steam Sale because it struck my eye and I was interested in this.

[h1] What is Orwell and how does it work you ask? [/h1]

Well, in general, "Orwell" is a game where you're supposed to stop crimes with the use of the new software called "Orwell" in a world that is set in our present. You were the chosen one for the new job as a government agent, alone and in charge of "Orwell". Your only direct communication is "Sykes", another agent speaking to you over a one-way-channel and evaluating your actions and decisions. At first, you're being introduced by a short cutscene about an incident that has just happened: a bombing. Now, your task as an anti-crime agent is to find out who committed the crime and later on arrest him or her. At first, you as the "Orwell"-Agent can observe target people (you start with one that was quite obvious in the opening) with the help of 3 programs: the Reader, something to browse news and websites with, the Listener, to eavesdrop on target people once you've collected their number, and finally the Insider, where you can actively browse through the target's personal computer, once again if you collected a certain data. At first you should be browsing through their "Timelines", a website that is similar to social media that we have, e.g. Facebook and Twitter, collecting basic information of them, something like their name, address, birth date and so on. These information are "datachunks" that you can upload to "Orwell" to fill out the targets profile, but you must be careful, as you will not be able to remove data once uploaded. You will get to know your target pretty fast pretty soon as you can observe everything they do online. Later on, there will be so-called "conflicting datachunks", which include at least 2 datachunks. If you choose one datachunk out of the conflicting pair and upload it, the other datachunk will be disabled, so you have to choose wisely once again. If you've done everything right and chose after your liking you will soon arrest your first suspect, great job! After successfully managing a day, you "log off" of "Orwell" and end your day, your work is over for today. As you progress through the episodes, you'll quickly realize how complicated your "first tutorial task" in your new job get and how everything is connected to each other, but I don't want to spoil all your fun.

"Orwell" features 5 episodes for one price in total, releasing 1 each week, and as of 11/11/2016, 4 episodes are already out.

[h1] Do I like it? [/h1]

I definitely do. It's not a very gameplay intensive game, but rather a point and click/drag game, with a bit of thinking involved, however, I think it's very relaxing and it features a packing story. Although, to fully understand the story you have to read everything you find, or you will only get half of the story, which is why I usually need around 90 mins for a full episode, decision making included. The game devs had a really great idea for a new video game and it's almost a bit frightening to decide, whether a person is guilty or not, only based on online data and the game also once again brings up the controversy about surveillance by the government, even in the most private sectors. I mean, you can read what they write to their closest friends and listen to their phone calls. Nonetheless, it's a very innovative game that I really enjoyed, also the soundtrack of the game fits the situation very well and overall, for a 10$ game, "Orwell" is a master piece. I really hope they release a second part of the game or more episodes.

I definitely RECOMMEND the game, and if you're still a bit unsure, you can still try the demo and see for yourself, before you make a decision.
Waiting every day for a new episode!

A really great game. It's kind of creepy if you thing about the main theme. But I'm eagerly waiting for each new episode.
The sneaky bit is that your, frankly simple action can cause huge problems for others. ANd all the time your feel like poking around in the dark, without getting a proper view of the hole picture.
A really good game!
Beautiful game!

Your choices DO influence the events that would happen later in the game, unlike some choices of some game dev companies.
ALSO, the events themselves are VERY powerful. They made me laugh, fell ashamed, shocked and angered! And this is rarely the case with me playing games!

So to wrap this up: INCREDIBLE. Must-have for all story-lovers.

That escalation in Episode 3, and The Episode 4 is even better....

What I really like in Orwell is how realistic people in the game react; it is almost as if I am the real surveillance operator. Very recommended for those who like intricate stories and innovative representation of games.

I bought this at PAX Aus, started playing it today with the intention of pacing myself... and 6 hours later I finished what was available.

CON
As with any story based game, once you're done, you're done. I'm not sure how much influence our choices have on the story progression but I'll try playing differently another time.

This game is just overall an enjoyable, immersive experience. While the theme of survelliance and invasion of privacy in the name of public safety is beaten over your head multiple times, its amazingly pleasant. The story is very easy to get into, and the UI keeps you in the game, the whole premise of the game is that you are working for government security from a computer, which keeps you plugged in. Personally, I would love to see if it would be possible to have multiple screens that involve your connections and profiles of suspect on one screen, and then have your articles, your listener, and your insider on another screen that can be easily switched to. However, just having a single screen and being able to read the chats and "hear" the conversations of other people is extremely realistic. Not only that, but the datachunks that progress the story feel diverse in that they can provide flavor text, progress the story-line, or cause an individual's background to seem more threatening then they actually are. The mystery of the game is also wonderful, making you guess who the perpetrators are and how much each person knows. There have been multiple moments in the episodes in which by utilizing the datachunks I am given I cannot help but feel like I am forcing people to be viewed as terrorist threats to the Nation, but we only get the side of the story that they post online and don't get to know what their real activities are.

Now the bad news: 
-The UI can be somewhat aggravating to navigate at times, and I wish there was a way to keep the reader open as you listened in on conversations.
-Not all new information immediately goes away when viewed and disabled, sometimes you will still have that star or red outline making you think there is more when in reality you have checked every single nook and cranny on the page.
- So much  flavor text, personally I feel as though there is a limit to how many extra articles there can be, and how much random news can be put in, but when you sit an read, its quite a lot. Granted, I understand they wanted to make the Nation seem much more realistic.

Despite these flaws, which are all honestly very subjective, this game is great fun and a must for people that love to be immersed in games for their story (and don't mind getting their head beat in about perspective and government spying).

Pros:
-Great Story
- Realistic lifestyles
- Diversity in choices
- Moral dilemmas

Cons: 
- Frustrating UI
- Sometimes faulty notification system

[h1]Preface[/h1]
This review is being written before the conclusion of the game in episode five. I've played through the first four episodes a couple times exploring different outcomes, however, as episode five is not out yet I'm not able to comment on the totallity of the story.

[h1]The Machine[/h1]
[b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] has a very close [url=http://www.cbs.com/shows/person_of_interest/]Person of Interest[/url] vibe. The government of the fictitious country has obtained a Machine, or System, that surveils the populous gathering information however it does not act on the gathered information. The idea of the game is that the system, aptly named [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b], isn't able to decern human subtlety, sarcasim, or deciet. As such, the fictious government has [b]outsourced[/b] the task of resolving conflicts in the data, and identifying what is relevant and what is not. You as the player take on this role as an outsider to the country, tasked with sifting through the data that [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] gives you access to inorder to identify person(s) of interest. This is a role somewhat like [i]Person of Interest[/i]'s Harold Finch.

[h1]What [i]Orwell[/i] Is Not[/h1]
I've seen several complaints that the game isn't challenging enough, many comparing it to several "hacker simulators" such as [b][i]Hacknet[/i][/b] or [b][i]UPLINK[/i][/b]. On the surface the concept might seem somewhat similar to games such as these, however, this is not what [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] is. In this game you are not doing any "hacking" or "cracking", that is [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b]'s job. You are more of a data analyst telling a hacker, that happens to be a computer system, what data is relevant and linked to certian people. Treating it in the same vein as other "hacker simulators" isn't fair to the game and if that is what you are expecting, you will be dissapointed.

[h1]What [i]Orwell[/i] Is[/h1]
So if [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] isn't a "hacker simulator" what is it? I've also seen the categorization as a "visual novel" which is much closer to what this game is. The game play is reminiscent of [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choose_Your_Own_Adventure]Choose Your Own Adventure[/url] books some of you might have read as a child. As such, the outcomes that occur in the game depend on what data you choose to "flag" or "link" to someone as relevant. This process will estabilsh relationships between persons of interest that may uncover new motivations, or might change the context of the data you have available. The game is about you being the guiding hand for a surveillance system tasked with preventing & solving crime.

[h1]Pros[/h1]
[list]
    [*]Interesting visual style
    [*]Enjoyable storyline that feels very linear (as it should), but leaves you with a sprinkling of "what if" moments where you feel things could have been different.
    [*]Fairly Intuitive gameplay.
[/list]

[h1]Cons[/h1]
[list]
    [*]Somewhat short, although there is some replay value if you want to try to achieve different outcomes from prior play through(s)
    [*]You aren't able to link data to someone until [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] identifies it as potentially relevant.
    [*]You aren't able to revise or change "known" data based on new information
    [*]You aren't able to alter "data conflicts" if you find additional information
    [*]No "Save Game" system, uses the idea of profiles instead to allow for differing play throughs
[/list]

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
The game is a fun and enjoyable experience if you do not have unrealistic expectations of what the game is and what the gameplay is like. It offers an interesting and thought provoking social commentary on the age of information technology that we live in. The game presents the idea of freedom & privacy -vs- surveillance & security in an interesting and fairly balanced way. If you actually think about what you are doing moment-by-moment in the game, you will likely find yourself re-evaluating your thoughts on these topics. That isn't to say this game is going to challenge your views or change your mind, simply that you will likely find yourself thinking about these topics and why you hold your views on these topics.

If you enjoy naritive driven experiences this game will likey fit well in your games library. While there are some things the game could certianly do better I didn't find these issues to detract significantly from the games main draw for me, it's story & premise. I would like to see the game updated with some sort of "Save Game" system that would allow you to "branch off" after each chapter within a single profile. This would make exploring different outcomes easier, howerver, I also can see that this goes against the linear nature of the games concept. The game strives to make you feel like you are participating in the events, that are time bound and as such linear in nature, which have consequences.

Overall I'm enjoying the game and would recommend it to those who enjoy adventure games, visual novels, and mysteries. This isn't really a problem/puzzle solving game (like a "hacker simulator") so if that is what you are looking for you may wish to pass on this game. I definitely recommend it for what it is and I'm really looking forward to the culmination of these events in episode five.

Can't wait to play this a second or third time and experiment with the system a little more, be more picky with what I reveal. Really great stuff so far. (Keep in mind that this is an episodic game, and as of this review the 5th episode hasn't been released.)

I bought Orwell straight away, as it's the kind of game I've been looking for since Uplink. 

It is really well designed and I got so absorbed in it that I played it twice and felt like I was really effecting the outcome of the game...including feeling incredibly guilty when I had made a mistake which effected others! I can't wait for the next few episodes and I'm gutted it's not going to be a longer/larger game as they have defo found a gap in the gaming market for this sort of thing. Great idea. Great game. I'm hooked!

The very small negative (literally because it's all I can think of) is that sometimes I come across characters involved in the investigation online before the game allows you too, because you're following a particular storyline. Which is fine, but a little frustrating when you want to add their photo to their file or a piece of information to Orwell that you've spotted but you're unable to select it because it's not in right order according to the storyline.

This game is more like a creatively-structured visual novel than anything else. Don't expect much in the way of puzzles or strategy. It's very linear. Reminds me a bit of Analogue.

That said, I like it. It's an immersive way to tell a story. The writing isn't the greatest but it does well enough. It accomplishes its goal of getting you caught up enough in what's going on that you later find yourself questioning how easily you made certain assumptions. 

I'm pretty invested in the story and I want to see where it goes. It's a little early to see how much your choices can effect things but I'm hoping that will result in different end states, since you essentially play information gatekeeper for the government, deciding what they do and do not see about the people you're snooping on.

In its current state, at 3 episodes, I think it would take most people about 2.5 hours to complete. Less if you didn't care about reading everything.

This is a really cool concept, but the clunky writing takes you out of it. I'd like to see it worked over with a lot more nuance. As it is, the storyline is kind of barebones and it diminishes the experience. I think it would be more immersive, and the writing could be forgiven, if things were a little more challenging.

All that said, the game also seems to be buggy?? I got stuck after Episode 1 and was unable to move forward because I couldn't upload information to its related profile. 

Maybe this'll just turn out to be an ironic revelation that I didn't get something in the game? Hope so.

EDIT: I think I came into this thinking it would be something else (like a strategy game), so my expectations were not met.

Quite impressive storytelling, but, frankly speaking, it's too easy to play in. You have not so much volume of data to work with and it... highlighted when it needs your attention.  It turns the analytics-skills game into the drag-n-drop simulator. Developers should improve it with some kind of "hints off" option. Do I recommend it? Yes, I do, but only if you want to waste some time like I do.

Three episodes in, and I absolutely adore this game. If you enjoy story-driven, dystopian games with a hint of puzzle-solving, you're going to love this mind-twisting comment on our Big Brother culture.
You're an investigator who needs to sort out datachunks to solve a crime that serves as a meta-reflection upon the government systems you serve yourself. The philosophical questions regarding surveillance and freedom are posed in an easy-to-digest manner, and you have to be very conscious of what sort of data you upload to the system: lives depend upon your choices, and even when you think you're right, there is always a consequence of your choice.
The gameplay interface is easy to use, the tutorial doesn't feel like a tutorial, the art style is beautiful, the characters all carry distinct voices, and the plot really leaves you second-guessing everything. It's a wonderful commentary on our own society, harkening back to George Orwell's 1984 with several quotes and achievements that borrow generously from the Orwellian vocabulary.
It reminds me a lot of Papers, Please, but without the time management. I can not recommend this enough.

I really want to like Orwell for the principle of trying to deliver a social media exploitation simulator, but ultimately, it's a flow-chart puzzle that only allows the player to progress once he or she has collected the necessary datachunks. This would be unobtrusive if the narrator (the guide) wasn't hovering over you at all times like an incompetent manager - instantly responding with positive or negative feedback. The game would be much better if you could upload information to something like a holding pool to review as a whole before submitting it to something like a file or record for the manager to review, but instead, the game flow pauses and continues with no continuity of real-time, even though the game desperately tries to emulate this moment of your day on the job . You might have a hunch about a suspect as you read information, so you would think to point out correlated characteristics, but nope, that doesn't matter because you can only upload information the game has already marked as valid.

Orwell is unique and immersive, so it does have that going for it, but the flow-chart progression heavily relies on the game being bug free. I hit a bug/glitch/design flaw in the second episode in which a datachunk in the suspects relationship field was not registering that I uploaded it. As a result, I was stuck. I poured over every bit of information for about three hours before I finally searched online for help and wound up uploading conflicting datachunks to do what I thought would fail the mission, but oh, how convenient, the game saves the day by holding my hand and progressing anyway. So, it’s more like an interactive novel than a social-engineering investigation simulator.

I've just played the first 3 episodes after buying a copy of this game from PAX Australia. I absolutely love games like this, where you get to snoop through people's social media and other electronic avenues of information to advance the story. In this game, you're part of the survelliance state, tasked with the ability to rummage through people's computer's, social media accounts, medical records etc to find out the identity of a domestic terrorist.

The gameplay is a little simplistic in that it involves a lot of reading and "uploading" certain relevant clues to people's profiles. But it's also compelling in the way the story unravels. There's also replayability since certain information you choose to upload will affect how the story will progress. I'd definitely be replaying it to see what other options exists.

The only other character you interact with, Stymes, is okay though for a government official, he seems a little panicked and jumps to conclusions sometimes. I don't mind it too much, it gives him personality (though you wonder how he'd gotten hired to his role in the first place).

The interface is clean, bright and easy to navigate. The music is simple but effective. The only suggestion I can make is that I wish there were ways to speed up the conversations you tap into, being the messaging and phone calls. You have to wait in real time for the messages to appear one after another, and I wish there's an option to make the text appear faster or instanteously, particularly for second playthroughs.

Can't wait for epiosdes 4 and 5!

This "game" is one of those video games that are more a Work of art than a simple vid3eo game. I have only played episode 1 to 4, and I am already impacted by what it really is. I can easily expect to learn several life skills and lessons from this game, and look forward to the intense and ever winding story that it presents.

So Orwell nails the game as an interface in the same way the Hacker series does.

You're not a gamer sitting at your desk, your an employee doing your job.

Your job in this case is to sift through information - and decide what to pass on / or what not to pass on to your superiors who will act on it.

What you do or don't do can have drastic differences in outcomes - and while the game highlights data chunks for you - there is critical information found in other places the game does not highlight for you.

Timing is also important - you may early on get some interesting new data, but it might turn out later to be a red herring or even wrong - so a careful thought out approach to your investigation matters.

I've played through the first three episodes twice - with different 'role play' mentalities - and the differences can be huge.

It's a relatively short game, but well worth the price of entry and a fascinating look at privacy, security and rights in the digital age.

If you liked games like Hacker, Floor 13 (oldie but goodie), Papers Please - you'll find a lot to like here.

Some typos might throw you a bit - but they kind of ad to the experience.

Highly recommended, and an excellent price for a polished experience.
Orwell is a good game with interesting puzzles and problem solving. I would reccomend this to anyone who enjoys thinking about what they're doing.

I don't normally write reviews, but I think I have to here. If you have any interest in narrative structure, or if you like detective novels, I strongly recommend this game.

The title may be somewhat misleading, as Orwell is not, in fact, set in a horrible dystopian nightmare future brought about by an overavundance of surveillance. In fact, The Nation seems like a pretty decent place to live.

You play an investigator operating the new "Orwell" surveillance system, the most advanced data trawler/compiler ever. It's your job to upload relevant information pertaining to a series of people who may be connected to a terrorist attack. Due to the Orwell Code of Ethics, only investigators are allowed to upload things to Orwell. As a result, based on what you upload, other characters will make some very important, potentially disastrous decisions.

The game plays at quite a sedate pace, allowing you plenty of time to mull over what would be the most accurate and relevant information to allow everyone to make the best decisions they can, which is nice. What's even better is that this really makes it incredibly tense when the game DOES put you on a (usually very short) timer and forces you to make a snap decision that could get people killed.

The narrative has pulled a few dick moves so far (mainly of the "Well that would have been good to know 30 seconds ago" variety), but none of them seem unfair, and they're entirely believable.

As a final big tick in my "things that make a good narrative game" box, the characters all act generally sensibly and behave as you would expect rational human beings in high stress situations to behave.

tl;dr - 10/10 would upload again.

Wow. 3 Episodes in, and I'm hooked. Will go into some detail in a moment, but let me start this with a warning:

If you play this game: TAKE. YOUR. TIME.
Don't power through it. Read everything. Let the narrative grab you, pull you in.
Then step away. For a day, perhaps two.
The episodes come out once a week -- and that gives you quite a bit of time to reflect on what you discovered, as well as the potential consequences of your actions.

That said, you'll read some reviews here that weigh heavily on the feelings that the game is effectively "on rails", and as a result this lends a very shallow narrative. Being that most of those were placed during only the first or second episode, of five, that's rather short-sighted. That being said, the narrative is NOT quick, and there is quite a bit to it that presumes you're going to fill in some of the holes. If you need full action to enjoy a game, this may not be a good fit for you.

Overall, Purely Subjective Score: 4.25/5

Storyline: 4/5
I've got a few quibbles. There are aspects to the story that are a bit too on the nose at times, pushing forward the big-brother aspect of the narrative, but overall, the slow burn aspect of the storyline as a whole is compelling. Despite that much of it is scripted, to the point that I really think that much of the illusion of control on the part of the player is exactly that -- an illusion, it doesn't take away from the overall story being told. You are a cog in the big mahcine that is Big Brother, in a far-more Orwellian nation-state, and you're taken on for the ride.

Art: 3/5
The art style here is exactly what is shown on the tin -- and while it gives the game a strange noir flavor, but there are aspects to it that are very displeasing from a purely aesthetic standpoint. I think it's mostly that it places me back in the days of heavy, visible polygon use in old games, which I'm frankly glad we've moved away from.

Verisimiltude: 3/5
This is fiction, pure and simple, but there are aspects to the tech that seems very magic/hand-wavey. I find myself wishing there was a bit more legitimacy to the tech you're supposed to be using.

Replayability: 4.5/5
There are a few mechanics within gameplay that are integral in giving the feeling that actions have consequences, and impact on the narrative. Some are small, others more significant (which I can't descibe without spoilers). Some details you highlight in-game are 'pointless' fluff, others can give the wrong (or right) perspective on a subject's motivations, and yet others can be clear conflicts in data that you have to choose between. All frame and connect the narrative. In some cases, this can lead to crimes being prevented (or not), people dying (or not), or the right/wrong accusation coming out in an interrogation. Remembering those, and seeing what happens if you go another route, can potentially lend to some completionist replays.

Overall? I encourage you to check this one out.

In Orwell, the devil's in the details.

On my first playthrough, I thought that this was just a visual novel. I thought that conflicting datachunks were no big deal; I mean, I can just upload one of them and both will be sent to Orwell. Right?

Well, I was wrong, and that resulted in some very real consequences.

See, most of the game involves reading articles and personal information about people. Orwell cherry-picks information it wants and you upload it. Some information is clearly false or misinterpreted by the machine, so you can choose not to upload those chunks.

But once you've been lured into a false sense of security, a conflicting datachunk pops up. You have to decide, from the options provided, which is the real story. That, I've learned, requires you to go back and cover everything you've read with a fine-toothed comb.

That's where the game gets tough. After three episodes, I have made one, and maybe two, clear-cut mistakes with disastrous consequences. I'm not sure what I missed, but that's the fun of the game. Be meticulous. Pay attention to every tiny detail. Think very carefully before you choose which story to endorse, because Orwell will take it as fact.

Orwell is an interesting game about collecting personal data from people through various means (social media, dating sites, phone calls etc.) and investigating to find the terrorist/s that plant bombs in public places. The gameplay reminds me a lot of Analogue : Hate Story, which is a good sign. Every document gives you new informations, that leads you to new documents etc.

Overall the writing is very solid and believable, you can only see typed messages but they all express the character's personality : the lawyer is writing slowly with perfect punctuation, the young activist uses slang and typos etc. Sometimes there are some blatant shortcuts designed for exposition (a conversation with an unknown person that starts with "What can I do for you, Susan Mills, my best friend from Hugand University ?") but it didn't bother me too much.

What bothers me however is how much the game holds your hand. You can only select a few informations and only about the suspect "du jour". Several times I thought "Wow, Alan is very suspect !" but I couldn't get any informations about him until the next day where I'm told "Today we'll focus on Alan, he's suspect". Am I the investigator or just a goddamn clerk ?

It led to a very aggravating moment where I had to chose between two options, I took the wrong one and innocent people died. To add insult to injury, my sidekick had the nerve to patronize me "What did we do wrong ? If we had taken the other option, this could have been avoided". I think it was meant to emotionally disturb me and make me think that this investigation method is fundamentally flawed, on top of being ethically reprehensible. But instead all I could think was "F*ck you, all informations you ALLOWED me to get pointed at the first option being the good one. You think you're cleverly ambiguous but you're just a cheap mystery novel deliberately misleading the audience to make the plot last long enough".

In conclusion, an extremely lukewarm approval, that might lead to a disapproval if they keep doing this in future episodes. I don't want to replay this game as it feels like Telltale's Walking Dead, where the illusion of choice disappears at the second playthrough where different choices don't impact as much as they seemed.

EDIT : I finished the 5 chapters, I keep my extremely uncommitted approval (lets say 50.1/100).
What limits this game the most is its linearity. I compared it to a mystery novel, it's even worse in late episodes, they want you to suspect specific people in specific orders punctuated by specific twists. You learn in chapter 5 crucial informations that you had no reason not to discover in chapters 1 and 2, since you follow the exact same protocol except the game deliberately kept informations away from you in order to make the game last 5 chapters.

The game also has the nerve to make this railroad look like a social commentary. "You've been chasing the wrong people the entire time, this is the proof that Orwell is unreliable !". Yeah but no, this is just proof that you're putting arbitrary limitations for the sake of the narrative. And even with that, Orwell did better than any other investigation method. Call it unethical, dangerous, tyrannical if you want, but it gets sh*t done and saved lives, and would have done even better without the railroad.

[h1] How far are you willing to go to protect the populace? [/h1]

[i]Orwell[/i] is a “visual novel” style game in which you have the ability to follow cyber-breadcrumbs in order to slowly uncover suspect’s online lives. Your goal? Stop a terrorist organization (?) from bombing public spaces. Your tools? As an agent, you are privy to the entirety of your target’s posts, articles, phone calls, emails, etc. Use this information to reveal more and more relevant webpages and conversations. The catch? You’re overlooked by a supervisor and you must choose what information to upload. This supervisor can only see the bits of information you feed him, so choose wisely or risk ruining an innocent’s life. The challenge? Upload only enough information to gain new leads, but not jump to conclusions. 

Are you really helping the greater good by invading the privacy of the few? Or have you caused more harm than good, muddling in affairs you should have never been in? Are the internet spies of today, really the superheroes of tomorrow? Find out by stepping into these large, cyber shoes. Act quickly and stop a harmful event in its tracks, or wait it out and discover it was a false alarm. Big brother is watching you. You are watching the people. Lives are on the line. Decide. 

Then watch as you say, [b]“I never meant for this to happen.”[/b]

Let me start off this review by saying I’m one who really enjoys a story-based game. I particularly enjoy consequence based story games (like [i]Telltale[/i]). If that’s not your cup of tea, this game is not for you. If you’re still interested, here’s the pros and cons for the game so far.

[h1]Pros:[/h1] [b]Interesting social commentary.[/b] There’s no denying that this is the age of technology, and with that comes a whole new slew of problems that our forefathers never could have foresaw when drafting the constitution. [i]Orwell[/i] heavily and obviously alludes to the current hot topics of freedom of internet access, government access to our personal files and correspondences, and general cyber security we see crop up in the news time and time again. 

[b]Easy interface.[/b] There’s not much to learn but drag and drop. Your un-uploaded data chunks are marked so you don’t lose track of what you’ve read, need to read, and are saving for later.

[b]More unique game flow.[/b] Events don’t happen unless you upload data chucks, leaving you to explore the branches of plot in whatever order feels natural to you. It does still feel a bit restricted, though, (see “A bit linear, limited” in cons) a perhaps more of a pseudo-free-directional choice. (But isn’t the concept of freedom what this game is all about?) 

[b]Intriguing artwork.[/b] The geometric artistic style lends itself to unconsciously nod its head towards the cyber-oriented world of the game. It ties in beautifully to the theme of the game—from the logo to the interface—without being too aggressive.

[h1]Cons:[/h1] [strike][b]A better save system!![/b][/strike] Update has added a rewind system, but I have not played since [strike]I cannot stress this enough. Since this is a consequence-based game, I’d like to be able to start from the end episode one, or so, with my decisions staying the same, and only make changes to my decisions from there out, with my profiles branching out from my first play through plot line. Starting over from the beginning is too much of a grind. Even a way to speed up messaging/call text on the second (and beyond) playthrough would be better for acheivement hunters or people just curious about the other endings. Examples of games with a good save system for this style of gameplay include [i]A Wolf Among Us[/i] and [i]Papers, Please.[/i][/strike]

[b]A bit linear, limited.[/b] There were some moments I wish some bit of text was highlighted (you may only drag and upload highlighted data chunks) since I wanted to explore that avenue of inquiry, but [i]Orwell[/i] had other plans. This gave the game a restricted feeling. It does not leave the game open to a world of naturally-occurring red herrings (only game-constructed ones, not user constructed), which I think would have added much more depth to the game. Also, it’s glaringly obvious which pieces of text carry great significance. (Those will be the ones with conflicting evidence) so sometimes the challenge of deciding to report information right away or wait was quite discernible, offering no challenge. Although, I will say that there are a few nuggets of data I uploaded without believing they would have as large of a consequence as they did. 

[b]Short.[/b] There’s only a little over forty minutes of game play per episode, and with five episodes, this leads to roughly four hours of gameplay (assuming you don’t replay events). I follow a rule of thumb of at least $1 to 1 hour of gameplay, so in that regard, it’s a bit pricey. Just wait for a sale. 

[h1]Remark:[/h1] [b]Play in one sitting[/b] (or as close to that as possible, if you don't have a full 4-5 hours to dedicate to one game) The flow and length of the game lends itself to be optimally played in one sitting. Taking a break and not have a comprehensive refresher (like the cinematic playbacks of key choices in [i]Telltale[/i] games) of your choices and actions is jarring to the enjoyment of the storyline in my opinion.

[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]
[b]I’d recommend buying [i]Orwell[/i] when on sale.[/b] It has an interesting and captivating storyline, despite some need of polishing. The interface, flow, and artwork lend itself to be an immersive experience into the lives of the people you are spying on to protect. Also, the current social commentary gives a real-world depth to the game. It does feel a bit restricting at times, and the story is short. The save system leaves much to be desired, since I would like to more easily explore all possibilities of my choices. But, despite these factors it was still enjoyable and fun to play.

This game is pretty fascinating, and I am looking forward to the next episodes (this is being released in episodes, bit by bit). Basically, you are being "Big Brother", hacking into personal files, browsing social media sites in order to solve and prevent crimes. 

Surely, there is a pretty obvious message here, which might be a bit too moralistic for some, but then again, I find it fascinating how you can actually upload unclear information (which is in conflict with another bit of information) and thereby push the investigation into the wrong direction.

Example: One guy mentions "torture", but didn't mean actual physical torture, but more like "it was torture to wait", more like in a fun way. However, if you pull that term and upload it, you will convince your superiors that the person is actually into torturing other people, thereby painting a totally wrong picture, distorting the facts. 
Which is what actually happens a lot, not only on the web, irl. 

The game has a certain indie, Papers Please type vibe... the focus here is on the storyline and your activities, and I think it's quite fascinating. The devs did well, letting you browse websites, hack into chats, wiretap phones, hacking desktops. Sure, it will eventually feel a bit "on rails", as you basically look for bits marked in blue and upload them, progressing the story with that, and the relevant bits are the only ones you can use and upload... so the game kind of leads you by the hand. All you do is read and scroll, find the info, drag it to the upload queue. 

However... I do think that a) if you bother to read what is going on, it might actually make you think a bit, and b) the story is pretty interesting, and I can't wait to see where all this leads. Really like the periodic release... every week, there is a new episode, which you are being told about by email.

Bottom-line
Great little game, eager to see more of it. Quite a bit of reading involved, but this game will make you think, it's an interesting take on the whole idea of Big Brother is watching you, and is quite well executed.

This game is so-so; I want to recommend something *like* Orwell, but I'm on the fence about recommending Orwell itself. The game raises interesting issues, and the world would indeed be better off if everyone had at least the simulated experience of working with a large-scale surveillance system. I even usually found the story compelling, and I finished the game. However, the execution also felt a little disappointing.

The main gameplay problem, in my experience, was that sometimes I felt forced to take random or stupid-seeming actions just to see what it was that would finally advance the plot. This was in spite of the "handholding" cues the game uses to help you along.

Another thing that bothered me was a set of accuracy/realism concerns, which I will go on about below.

*************************************************

(Optional section about accuracy)

My main objection is that the game gives a poor sense of what doing an investigation with help of an Orwell-like system would actually be like in real life. In real life, either A) the computer would be a very powerful autonomous system and would make conclusions without human or involvement; or B) the human researcher would have sensible basic capabilities such as updating information, correcting machine-extracted snippets, and supplementing files with written analysis. The game tries to be somewhere in between, and in the process makes something that's unrealistic and sometimes annoying.  Also, there were also moments of "what the heck does the game want from me now", when I would add pointless or even incorrect information to the Orwell database solely to see if it would finally be the thing to move the plot forward.

The fact that you can't modify information in the Orwell crime database is pretty stupid on the face of things. To be fair, though, maybe it stands metaphorically for problems that could actually arise. For example, if two government agencies had a file on you, but the two were not in sync, the fact that you're not actually a criminal could be updated in one department's file without the second department learning about this, and perhaps the second database could lead to your extrajudicial killing.

The contextless, overaly literal way that information is passed from investigator to police is completely absurd. Perhaps this is a useful reflection of one possible way that an agency using an Orwell-type system could be dysfunctionally structured, though you'd hope that a bureaucracy wouldn't be quite that stupid. Or perhaps this limited information passing is symbolic of a potentially problem where two crime databases were linked, but could only communicate back and forth using a limited, contextless technical vocabulary, which would perpetuate misunderstanding. 

Perhaps the point of the game, though, is not to be right about the *particulars* of what could go wrong in a mass surveillance system, but more to give people an accessible experience that gives a general sense of creepiness.

Just played through Episodes 1-3.

A very interesting game, most titles in this situation would have you playing as the revolutionist trying to overthrow Big Brother or undermine it in some rebellious way. The story is deep and rich keeping you enthralled as you find out more and more about each character and the spider web that forms connecting them all.

The graphics are simplistic but it doesn't need a fancy 3D 60fps affair as a game like this isn't about pushing the boundaries in that department. In some ways I would say this is sort of like a 2D version of Life Is Strange in that you feel like you are the creator of the story and that the choices you are making truly affect the characters and story arc.

In short I would highly recommend this game, I don't know how long it will take to complete, possibly 4-5 hours maybe? But the story is well worth the £6.99.

The premise is simple:
It's a game where you play a investigator who works for the government, sifting through data in all of its forms in order to fight for the safety of the public in the fictional world that it's set in.

There have been many 'hacking' games that have come out over the years, but Orwell takes the idea and puts you in the position of 'good' rather than 'bad', which creates the core ideology of the game -- If what you're doing is so good, then why do you feel so bad doing it?

The game proceeds along a UI of sorts, one that allows you to sift through websites, personal pages and even listen on some incredibly well-simulated 'real time chats', along with interruptions and intentional spelling errors that betray the typer's emotions and mental states. It's one of the best simulations of texting I've seen before in a game, and it DOES stand out. The articles and websites, while simple and clean, are detailed and packed full of worldbuilding -- the developers go out of their way to fill the world with detail that was never necessary to get from point A to B, but still fill everything with life and activity, and the world ends up feeling a little bit less compartmentalized than other games which force you into a limited POV.

However, this all leads back to the internal condundrum I have with this game:
You work with a handler who analyses the information you send him, and it's his job to make sense of it all. All you do is forward him the pertinent information, enough for him to make decisions and calls on how to handle situations. And you must choose what it is you want to send.

It's your choice to pick A over B. And it's not outright lies, because you're the good guy, remember? But whatever you send can tinge a thought, affect outcomes and colour perceptions in slight, yet pertinent, ways. Your own analysis plays a big part in how you want to portray someone else, and ultimately, the only one who has to live with the decisions you make is yourself.

Orwell is a great game about people, but more than that, it's a platform to help you examine yourself as a person. Since you're doing this for the percieved good, what decisions will you make and how far will you go to get what you want? And is there ever a time when personal freedom can be infringed upon for the greater result? Well... that might be another question for another time.

It's a good game tho, eh?

(( P.S.: Like any other 'visual novel' style game, and including the horrendous works of Mr. David Cage, I am fully aware that some of these 'choices' may be nothing more than illusionary. However, the game does it well enough in its context that reflecting upon the choices you make actually makes more than just a surface-level difference since you're playing not a character, but yourself. And considering the game's name and influences, I believe this to be the point. ))
